title: Evolution of Flood Exposure Under Social Heterogeneity: Insights From Large‐Scale Agent‐Based Modeling
content:
Abstract

Flood risk is unevenly distributed and repeated flood exposure among marginalized households is associated with constrained recovery and persistent poverty. Most socio-hydrological models represent behavioral diversity through a limited set of attributes rather than the socio-economic composition of the population, limiting explanations of how risk persists and is redistributed across society. This study develops a geospatial agent-based model (ABM) that simulates flood exposure and hazard-induced migration of nearly 100,000 households per simulation in the Brahmaputra floodplain, Assam, India. Four behavioral archetypes (Engineers, Hardened Preparers (HP), Discontents, and Pessimists) are derived from socio-economic characteristics including social group, asset ownership, income source, and education. These archetypes exhibit distinct preferences for relocation, in situ coping, and settlement near levees, spanning heterogeneous adaptation pathways under varying flood exposure. The model reproduces levee effect and demonstrates how undefended regions face greater impacts from frequent floods, while defended regions accumulate higher exposure during rare extremes. In defended regions, social heterogeneity drives divergent risk trajectories; only 31.7% of Engineers exceed exposure thresholds, compared to 72.2% of Pessimists. HP and Pessimists often remain trapped in high-hazard areas for over a decade, whereas Engineers and Discontents typically relocate after 5 to 6 years. However, mobility does not eliminate risk, as climate change intensifies hazards. Under SSP5, exposed households increase by nearly 40% for Engineers and Discontents, but only by 6.6% and 11.6% for HP and Pessimists, respectively. Long-term flood risk thus emerges from interaction among behavioral heterogeneity, structural protection, and social inequality, underscoring the need for equity-sensitive flood management.
